title: Ang 1193–1196: Basant's Bhagats
tomorrow: it's noon and it's hot. what does the Granth sing at midday?

lines: PLACES TO SEE BEFORE YOU DIE.
cards: Every feed has its list of places to see before you die: a mountain, a temple, a beach at sunrise. Somewhere in Basant, on ang 1195, a saint named Ramanand is getting ready for a trip like that.
He grinds sandalwood, mixes in fragrant oils, and sets out to worship at God's own place. And then he doesn't go. He stays home.
Sikh readers still talk over what that means. Why does he stay?

teach.b: Basant closes with the Bhagats: Kabir, Ramanand, Namdev and Ravidas. Ramanand's hymn sits among them. In paraphrase: where would I go?
I'm colored at home. My mind won't wander off; it's settled. One day a longing rose in me; I ground sandalwood with fragrant oils and set out to worship at God's place.

teach.h: THE GURU SHOWED ME: IN MY MIND.
teach.b: The Guru showed me that God was in my own mind. Wherever I go, I find water and stone; you fill everything, equally. Sikh readers hear two things in this.
Some hear a door closing on pilgrimage as a way to earn anything. Water and stone are water and stone; the color is already at home, in the mind the Guru opens.

teach.h: ONE VIEW: NO TRIP EARNS IT.
teach.b: On this view, a long trip to a holy pool can quietly teach the wrong lesson, that God lives over there.
Others point out that Sikhs still travel to Darbar Sahib and the historic gurdwaras, and say the hymn is about why you go, not whether.
Go to hear kirtan, to sit with the sangat, to wash dishes in the langar, and you're not chasing God over there; you're coming home more colored than you left. Both readings take Ramanand at his word.
Both end in the same place: the color isn't stored in a building. Colored at home.

how: Sikhs travel to Darbar Sahib in Amritsar and to historic gurdwaras for kirtan, sangat and seva, and also hold that the Name can be found anywhere; Ramanand's Basant hymn is sung in kirtan and quoted on both sides of the question.

o: where Basant's Bhagats begin, Ramanand among them
where Guru Nanak opens the raga of spring
where the ninth Guru's spring hymns begin

p: set out with sandalwood, stayed home
what he finds wherever he goes
no trip earns what's already home
it's why you go, not whether

s: Ramanand's hymn tells of setting out to worship with sandalwood
he ground sandalwood with fragrant oils and set out; the Guru showed him God in his own mind.
Sikh readers all agree that this hymn rules out visiting historic gurdwaras
some hear it setting pilgrimage aside; others hear it about why you go, not whether.
Ramanand says God lives only at home
he says you fill everything, equally; the color is at home because God is everywhere.

games.q: a friend says, "a trip to Darbar Sahib is basically tourism. Ramanand stayed home." you love those trips. before you answer, what's the strongest version of her view?
o: Ramanand set out to worship and found God in his own mind: the holy isn't somewhere you travel to.
Ramanand says gurdwaras are no better than temples, so neither one is worth visiting.
the Granth forbids every trip to a holy place, so the trip breaks a rule.
games.why: that's her best case, straight from the hymn. the other side's best case is just as real: go for the kirtan and sangat, and come home colored.

practice: Say Ramanand's question out loud, slowly, in English: where would I go? I'm colored at home. Then stay exactly where you are for the sit, and let where you are be enough.
If you'd like, read ang 1195 before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Ang 1193. Where Basant's Bhagats begin, and Ramanand, ready for a pilgrimage, finds God in his own mind.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: rang, color, the dye of love Ramanand says he's colored with at home.

carryVoice: Colored at home: whether you travel or stay, the color isn't stored in a building. That's Basant done.
